provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Addition with carrying
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify addition with carrying.
The pupils should be able to solve addition problems with carrying.

Introduction:
We know how to add small numbers.
Today we add bigger numbers.

Content:
Addition with carrying means we have more than ten in a column.
We use sticks for ones and bundles for tens.
For 27 plus 15, we put 7 sticks and 5 sticks together.
That makes 12 sticks. We take 10 sticks and make a bundle.
We write 2 in the ones place and carry the bundle to the tens.
Now we add 2 bundles and 1 bundle and the carried bundle.
That makes 4 bundles. So 27 plus 15 is 42.

Class activity:
Each pupil gets 27 sticks and 15 sticks.
Count them and make bundles when you have ten.

Evaluation questions:
What is 18 plus 15?
What do we do when we have ten ones?
Solve 25 plus 17.

Summary:
When we add and get ten or more, we carry a bundle to the next column.

topics.title: Subtraction with borrowing
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify subtraction with borrowing.
The pupils should be able to solve subtraction problems with borrowing.

Introduction:
We know how to take away small numbers.
Today we take away from bigger numbers.

Content:
Subtraction with borrowing means we don't have enough ones to take away.
We use sticks for ones and bundles for tens.
For 42 take away 17, we look at the ones place.
We have 2 sticks but need to take away 7 sticks.
We borrow one bundle from the tens place.
Now we have 12 sticks. We take away 7 sticks and have 5 left.
We now have 3 bundles left. So 42 take away 17 is 25.

Class activity:
Each pupil has 42 sticks in bundles and sticks.
Take away 17 sticks and see what is left.

Evaluation questions:
What is 53 take away 28?
What do we do when we don't have enough ones?
Solve 61 take away 34.

Summary:
When we can't take away enough ones, we borrow a bundle from the tens.

topics.title: Word problems 1
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to listen to a word problem.
The pupils should be able to draw a picture of a word problem.
The pupils should be able to solve addition word problems.

Introduction:
We know how to add numbers.
Today we add things in stories.

Content:
Word problems are stories with numbers.
We need to find the numbers in the story.
For example: There are 5 birds in a tree.
3 more birds come. How many birds are there now?
We see we need to add 5 and 3.
We can draw 5 birds and then 3 more birds.
Then we count all the birds to get the answer.
Another example: Ako has 7 flowers.
Ade gives him 4 more flowers. How many flowers does Ako have now?
We add 7 and 4 to get 11.

Class activity:
The teacher tells a story about birds and flowers.
Pupils draw the story and solve it.

Evaluation questions:
What is the first number in the story?
What do we do when we see 'more' in a story?
Solve: Bola has 3 pencils. Tunde gives her 5 pencils. How many pencils does Bola have?

Summary:
In word problems, we find the numbers and decide whether to add or take away.

topics.title: Word problems 2
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to listen to a subtraction word problem.
The pupils should be able to write a sentence for a word problem.
The pupils should be able to solve subtraction word problems.

Introduction:
We know how to take away numbers.
Today we take away in stories.

Content:
Word problems can also be about taking away.
For example: There are 9 oranges on a table.
Ayo eats 3 oranges. How many oranges are left?
We see we need to take away 3 from 9.
We can write the sentence: 9 take away 3 equals?
Then we solve to get 6.
Another example: There are 15 children in a class.
7 children go home. How many children are left in class?
We take away 7 from 15 to get 8.

Class activity:
The teacher tells a story about taking away.
Pupils write the sentence and solve it.

Evaluation questions:
What do we do when we see 'left' in a story?
Write a sentence for: There are 12 eggs. 4 eggs break. How many eggs are left?
Solve: There are 20 sweets. 8 sweets are eaten. How many sweets are left?

Summary:
In take away stories, we find the starting number and subtract what is taken away.

topics.title: Multiplication as groups
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify groups.
The pupils should be able to make equal groups.
The pupils should be able to solve simple multiplication problems.

Introduction:
We know how to add numbers together.
Today we learn about groups.

Content:
Multiplication is about making equal groups.
For example: Two groups of five means we have two groups with five in each group.
We can write this as 2 times 5.
We can also think of rows and columns.
Like in a market, you might have rows of yams.
If there are 3 rows with 4 yams in each row, that is 3 times 4.
We count all the items to get the answer.
3 times 4 is 12 because 4 plus 4 plus 4 equals 12.

Class activity:
The teacher gives pupils counters and asks them to make groups.
For example: Make 3 groups of 4 counters each.
Then count how many counters there are altogether.

Evaluation questions:
What does 2 groups of 3 mean?
How many are in 4 groups of 2?
Draw 3 groups of 5 and count them.

Summary:
Multiplication is counting equal groups quickly.

topics.title: Division as sharing
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to share items equally.
The pupils should be able to solve simple division problems.

Introduction:
We know how to make groups.
Today we learn about sharing.

Content:
Division is about sharing things equally.
For example: Share 12 sweets to 3 friends.
Each friend should get the same number of sweets.
We give one sweet to each friend until all sweets are shared.
Each friend gets 4 sweets.
We can write this as 12 divided by 3 equals 4.
Another example: Share 8 oranges to 2 children.
Each child gets 4 oranges because 8 divided by 2 equals 4.

Class activity:
The teacher gives pupils 12 counters and asks them to share equally among 3 friends.
Pupils should give one counter at a time to each friend until all are shared.

Evaluation questions:
What does 'share equally' mean?
Share 10 pencils to 2 children.
Solve: 15 divided by 3 equals?

Summary:
Division is sharing things equally among friends.

topics.title: Patterns and sequences
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify a pattern.
The pupils should be able to continue a number pattern.

Introduction:
We know how to count numbers.
Today we learn about patterns.

Content:
A pattern is something that repeats.
In number patterns, numbers follow a rule.
For example: 2, 4, 6, 8.
The rule is add 2 each time.
So the next number is 10.
Another pattern: 5, 10, 15, 20.
The rule is add 5 each time.
So the next number is 25.
We can also have patterns with shapes or colors.

Class activity:
The teacher claps a pattern and pupils repeat it.
Then the teacher says a number pattern and pupils continue it.

Evaluation questions:
What comes next in 3, 6, 9, 12?
What is the rule for 10, 20, 30, 40?
Continue this pattern: 1, 3, 5, 7, ?

Summary:
Patterns have rules that help us find what comes next.

topics.title: Symmetry fun
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify symmetrical shapes.
The pupils should be able to create symmetrical designs.

Introduction:
We know about shapes and patterns.
Today we learn about symmetry.

Content:
Symmetry means both sides are the same.
A butterfly has symmetrical wings.
If you draw a line down the middle, both sides match.
We can make symmetrical pictures by folding paper.
Fold the paper in half and draw on one side.
Then unfold and see how the other side matches.
We can also use objects like leaves or buttons to make symmetrical designs.

Class activity:
Each pupil gets a piece of paper folded in half.
They draw on one side and then unfold to see the symmetrical picture.

Evaluation questions:
What does symmetry mean?
Show a symmetrical object in the classroom.
Draw a symmetrical shape.

Summary:
Symmetry means both sides are the same when you fold them.

topics.title: Mental maths
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to solve addition problems quickly.
The pupils should be able to solve subtraction problems quickly.

Introduction:
We know how to add and take away.
Today we do it quickly in our heads.

Content:
Mental maths means solving problems in your head.
We don't use paper or counters.
For example: What is 5 plus 3?
We can count up from 5: 6, 7, 8.
So 5 plus 3 is 8.
For subtraction: What is 9 take away 4?
We can count down from 9: 8, 7, 6, 5.
So 9 take away 4 is 5.
We can use tricks like doubles or near doubles.

Class activity:
The teacher sets a timer for 1 minute.
Pupils solve as many addition problems as they can before the timer rings.

Evaluation questions:
What is 7 plus 5?
What is 10 take away 3?
Solve these quickly: 6 plus 4, 8 take away 2, 9 plus 1.

Summary:
Mental maths is solving problems quickly in our heads.

topics.title: Revision and graduation maths show
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to solve various maths problems.
The pupils should be able to explain how they solved a problem.

Introduction:
We have learned many maths things this term.
Today we show what we know.

Content:
We will revise addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.
We will also revise word problems, patterns and symmetry.
Each pupil will come to the front and solve a problem.
They will explain how they got their answer.
After the show, pupils who try hard will get Maths Star certificates.

Class activity:
The Maths Show: Each pupil solves one problem on the board.
They explain their method to the class.

Evaluation questions:
Solve 25 plus 17.
What comes next in 2, 4, 6, 8?
Share 12 sweets to 3 friends.

Summary:
We have learned many maths things this term and we are proud of our work.
